script: Some zoos give baby cheetahs a literal best friend - a puppy - because cheetahs are one of the most anxious big cats there is. In 1976, at an Oregon wildlife park, researcher Laurie Marker was hand-raising a lonely cheetah cub named Khayam, with no other cheetahs around. On a hunch, she paired Khayam with a puppy named Shesho - and it worked instantly, calming the cub almost immediately. Khayam became the first cheetah conservation ambassador, touring the country with her best friend by her side. Researchers later confirmed it: cheetahs in captivity show real, measurable stress that wild cheetahs don't have. The idea caught on. Zoos nationwide now pair cheetah cubs with puppies, introduced when both are just weeks old. At the Columbus Zoo, a cheetah named Emmett and a Labrador named Cullen were inseparable for years after being paired as cubs. Nearly 50 years later, it's still standard practice - because even the fastest animal on Earth sometimes just needs a good friend. Follow for more true stories with a twist nobody expects.

metadata.title: Random But True: Why Zoos Give Cheetahs Their Own Emotional Support Dog
metadata.caption:
1976, a wildlife park in Oregon. Researcher Laurie Marker was hand-raising a lonely cheetah cub named Khayam - with no other cheetahs around to keep her company.

On a hunch, she paired Khayam with a puppy named Shesho. It worked instantly, calming the cub almost immediately. Khayam went on to become the first cheetah conservation ambassador, touring the country with her best friend by her side.

Researchers later confirmed why it works: cheetahs in captivity show real, measurable stress that wild cheetahs simply don't have.

The idea caught on nationwide. Zoos now pair cheetah cubs with puppies - usually Labradors, Golden Retrievers, or Anatolian Shepherds - introducing them when both are just weeks old. At the Columbus Zoo, a cheetah named Emmett and a Labrador named Cullen were inseparable for years after being paired as cubs in 2016.

Nearly 50 years after Khayam and Shesho, it's still standard practice at zoos across the country.
